title: Helm and Kustomize: Packaging and Deploying to Kubernetes
summary: Quick revision notes on Helm charts, values, templates and the release lifecycle, Kustomize bases, overlays and patches, and how to choose between them.

chapters.title: Helm Charts, Values and Templates
points: A chart is a package of Kubernetes manifest templates plus metadata; layout: Chart.yaml (name, version, appVersion), values.yaml (defaults), templates/, charts/ (dependencies), _helpers.tpl (named partials)
Mechanism: helm renders Go templates in templates/ with values merged from values.yaml, then -f files, then --set (later wins), and sends the resulting YAML to the cluster

Template syntax: {{ .Values.image.tag }}, {{ .Release.Name }}, {{ .Chart.Name }}; pipelines like {{ .Values.name | default "app" | quote }}; conditionals {{ if .Values.ingress.enabled }}; loops {{ range .Values.env }}
chart version vs appVersion: version is the chart package version (bump on any chart change); appVersion is the app's own version and is informational only
Example: helm create myapp scaffolds a chart; helm template myapp ./myapp -f prod.yaml renders locally without touching the cluster; helm lint ./myapp checks it
Mistake: wrong indentation of included YAML; use {{ toYaml .Values.resources | nindent 12 }} instead of pasting text
Mistake: --set on a list or nested key is awkward and error-prone; prefer a values file, and quote strings that could parse as numbers or booleans

chapters.title: Helm Install, Upgrade, Rollback and Releases
points: A release is one named installation of a chart in a namespace; the same chart can be installed many times under different release names
Helm 3 stores release state as Secrets in the release namespace (sh.helm.release.v1.<name>.v<revision>); there is no Tiller; each upgrade creates a new revision
Install: helm install web ./myapp -n prod --create-namespace -f prod.yaml; the idempotent form is helm upgrade --install web ./myapp -f prod.yaml
Upgrade and rollback: helm upgrade web ./myapp --set image.tag=1.4; helm history web lists revisions; helm rollback web 2 creates a new revision with revision 2's config
Inspect and remove: helm list -A, helm status web, helm get values web (add --all for defaults too), helm get manifest web, helm uninstall web
Safe deploys: --atomic rolls back automatically on failure (implies --wait); --wait blocks until resources are ready; --timeout sets the limit; helm diff upgrade (plugin) previews changes
Mistake: helm upgrade without --reuse-values or the original -f resets overrides to chart defaults; always pass the same values files each time

chapters.title: Kustomize Bases, Overlays and Patches
points: Kustomize is template-free customization of plain YAML, built into kubectl; every directory with a kustomization.yaml is a unit listing resources and transformations
Base holds the common manifests; an overlay (e.g. overlays/prod) references the base under resources: and layers environment-specific changes on top without editing the base
Layout: base/{deployment.yaml,service.yaml,kustomization.yaml} and overlays/{dev,prod}/kustomization.yaml with resources: [../../base]

Built-in transformers: namePrefix/nameSuffix, namespace, commonLabels, images (change name/tag), replicas, configMapGenerator and secretGenerator (append a content hash suffix so changes trigger rollouts)

Patches: patches: with a path or inline target selector; strategic merge patch merges fields by structure (containers matched by name); JSON 6902 patch uses op/path/value for precise add, replace or remove
Preview with kubectl kustomize overlays/prod (or kustomize build); apply with kubectl apply -k overlays/prod; delete with kubectl delete -k
Mistake: a strategic merge patch with a mismatched metadata.name or kind matches nothing and is silently ignored; commonLabels also changes immutable selectors, which can break existing Deployments

chapters.title: Choosing Between Helm and Kustomize
points: Helm: templating and packaging with versioned releases, rollback, hooks and a chart repository ecosystem; best for distributing third-party software and parameterized apps
Kustomize: patch-based, no templating language, output stays valid YAML, no release tracking or built-in rollback; best for your own manifests with per-environment differences
Comparison: Helm = Go templates + values + release history; Kustomize = base + overlays + patches, no state stored in the cluster
Typical choice: install third-party apps (ingress-nginx, cert-manager, Prometheus) with Helm; manage in-house services with Kustomize overlays per environment

They combine: helm template ... | kubectl apply -f - then patch the output with Kustomize, or use helmCharts in kustomization.yaml (needs kustomize build --enable-helm); GitOps tools like Argo CD and Flux support both
Mistake: mixing ownership, such as using kubectl apply -k on resources a Helm release owns, causes drift and conflicting field managers; pick one tool per resource

chapters.title: Helm and Kustomize Cheat Sheet
points: Helm: helm create, lint, template, install, upgrade --install, list, status, history, rollback, uninstall
Helm values precedence: chart values.yaml < -f files (in order) < --set; helm get values shows what is applied
Helm safety flags: --atomic, --wait, --timeout, -n ns, --create-namespace, --dry-run --debug
Kustomize: kubectl kustomize <dir>, kubectl apply -k <dir>, kubectl delete -k <dir>
kustomization.yaml keys: resources, namePrefix, namespace, images, replicas, configMapGenerator, patches
Rule of thumb: Helm for packaged or third-party apps, Kustomize for plain in-house YAML per environment
